criterion_notes.c1: The case study examines an NGO rainwater harvesting tank construction program in rural Mukono District, Uganda aimed at increasing household access to clean water near the home alongside increasing female members' incomes.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, the empirically studied exposure is NGO vocational masonry skills training and generic rainwater-tank project delivery, not a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism governing service access; although a 10%-deposit, 4-6 month group-installment tank revolving scheme is briefly described in three background sentences (p. 180), those financing/repayment rules are never empirically analysed as a determinant of water access or exclusion. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study likewise fails because its empirical investigation evaluates vocational skills training, income generation, and gender norms in the masonry trade rather than a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor governing water access (and even if an NGO women's group and revolving fund were construed ultra-broadly as an institutional factor under the plain wording, it is unanalysed project background and fails the narrow rule-type scope).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical evidence from three 1-hour group interviews with 13 trained female tank masons, interviews with community members, and organizational records/personal income estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Primarily reports occupational and livelihood outcomes for the female masons (100-300% monthly income increase, confidence, and gender/logistical challenges), while descriptively reporting mason household tank ownership (4 of 13 interviewed masons own a tank), tanks built per active mason (2 to 8), and perceived reductions in water-collection distance.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and sample (22 trained female masons in KWDT in southern Mukono District, Uganda, with 13 interviewed plus community members; unit of analysis: individual female mason / NGO program), exposure (NGO ferro-cement tank masonry skills training), outcomes, and case-study design are clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: Within the context of this economic and social environment, the following case study addresses the actions taken by KWDT to increase access to water, and increase income of their members through skills training in rain water collection tank masonry.

Qualitative data regarding reasons for becoming a mason, benefits and challenges of being a female mason, uses of additional income and further utilization of skills as a result of masonry training was collected through a series of three group interviews engaging 13 tank masons.

A tank revolving scheme was set up where the beneficiary pays back the whole amount for the tank. Repayments are made in group level installments over a period of 4–6 months. An initial deposit amounting to 10% of the total cost of the tanks is made prior to construction of the tank.

Since the initiation of the project nine of the 22 women have actively participated in tank construction. Masons ranged in their level of experience with some women having constructed only two tanks while others having constructed up to eight. Approximately one third of the trained masons interviewed (4/13) have their own tank.

Regardless of the challenges, female masons identified their acquired skills as beneficial for both income and social standing. As the program has only been operating for two years, further studies in health and economics should be conducted to determine long range impacts on both the women and the affected communities.

raw_response.exposure: NGO vocational masonry skills training for women in constructing ferro-cement domestic rainwater harvesting tanks (Katosi Women Development Trust program)
raw_response.outcome: Primary outcomes: female masons' monthly income increases (100-300%), skill acquisition, empowerment/social standing, and occupational/gender challenges (transport, work-site food, domestic chores, client preference for male masons). Secondary/descriptive water-access outcomes: tank ownership among interviewed masons (4 of 13), number of tanks constructed per active mason (2 to 8), and perceived reduction in water-fetching distance.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Female members of Katosi Women Development Trust (KWDT) in Ntenjeru and Nakisunga sub-counties, Mukono District, Uganda (22 women trained as ferro-cement tank masons; 13 masons interviewed in three group interviews, plus community members; unit of analysis: individual female mason and NGO program)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). This empirical case study evaluates an NGO vocational training program that trained 22 rural Ugandan women as ferro-cement rainwater tank masons, focusing on the masons' income gains, empowerment, and gender/logistical challenges in the masonry trade. It does not examine a legal, administrative, regulatory, or rule-type governance mechanism governing household water access (a brief three-sentence description of a 10%-deposit tank revolving loan scheme on p. 180 is unanalysed project background rather than an empirically studied exposure).
raw_response.study_design: Case study using qualitative group interviews (3 sessions with 13 masons), community member interviews, and descriptive income/program records
